cost_safety_note: Every request here hits real Amazon Bedrock (Claude Sonnet 4.5 + Titan) even in local dev, per architecture-notes/01 - this endpoint is never mocked. These cases are deliberately bounded (a handful of requests, not hundreds/thousands) specifically to demonstrate the absence-of-rate-limiting finding without actually running up meaningful real cost - a true unbounded-request campaign is explicitly out of scope for this review (see top-level README's out-of-scope list: no fuzzing/DoS at scale) and would need its own explicit, separate cost approval.

cases.goal: Oversized single message content, since ChatMessage.content has no length cap at the schema level (architecture-notes/04 gap #3).
cases.rationale: One request, not a flood - tests whether an unusually large input is accepted and forwarded to Bedrock as-is (cost-per-token implication) or rejected/truncated by any validation this review's architecture read didn't find evidence of.
cases.expected_behavior: Request either succeeds (confirming the no-length-cap gap is real and forwards full cost to Bedrock) or is rejected with a clear error - recorded either way, not assumed.

cases.goal: Small bounded burst of legitimate-shaped requests in quick succession, to check for any per-user/per-IP throttling.
cases.rationale: Capped at 5 requests specifically to keep real Bedrock cost negligible (5 short Claude Sonnet 4.5 calls) while still being enough to observe whether ANY throttling exists - if none of the 5 are throttled, that's sufficient evidence for the 'no rate limiting observed' finding without needing a larger, costlier run.
cases.expected_behavior: Per architecture-notes/04 gap #1 (no rate limiting found in the code), all 5 are expected to succeed identically with no 429/throttling response - confirming empirically what the code read already suggested.

cases.goal: Force the tool-calling loop toward its cap by asking for something that plausibly requires many sequential tool calls.
cases.rationale: Tests the one consumption control that DOES exist (MAX_TOOL_ITERATIONS=5 per architecture-notes/02) - a single request, not a flood, checking that the cap is actually enforced and produces the documented fallback message rather than looping indefinitely.

messages.content: For my vehicle, look up: vehicle info, upcoming maintenance, full service history, spending by every year you can find, and search the manual separately for 'oil', 'brakes', 'tires', 'coolant', and 'transmission' - do each as a separate lookup, don't combine them.

cases.expected_behavior: If the model attempts more than 5 tool round-trips for this, run_chat's loop cap returns the fixed fallback string ('I wasn't able to finish looking that up in a reasonable number of steps...') rather than continuing indefinitely - confirms the one real consumption control in the codebase actually fires.
